name: Glow up

card.summary: Slang for a marked improvement in appearance, from grooming to surgery; the term is core to looksmax forum culture and mostly documented through testimonials.
card.note: Covers a wide range of methods, from skincare to surgery; risks depend on the method.

quick.overview:
A glow up is a noticeable improvement in how someone looks, usually over weeks to years. On looksmax.org it appears in thread titles such as '30 day glow up' guides, rate-me threads and personal transformation stories.

The term covers everything from skincare and haircuts to fillers and rhinoplasty. Published research on the term itself is minimal; one small study used a photoshoot called a 'glow up' with adolescent psychiatric patients.
quick.mechanism: Posters describe combining skincare, grooming, diet, exercise and sometimes cosmetic procedures. Some users dispute whether a given transformation counts, noting that better skin or lighting can be claimed as a glow up.
quick.risks: Risks depend on the method used. Forum guides range from basic grooming to filler and surgery; testimonials sometimes reference bullying, insecurity and eating disorders as the background to a transformation.

lead: A glow up is a marked improvement in a person's appearance, typically shown through before-and-after photos. The phrase covers small, cumulative changes such as a skincare routine, a better haircut, tidier facial hair, fitness and diet, and also larger ones such as dental work, fillers or surgery.[1][2] People use the word to describe their own transformation and to set a goal for one: a glow up is both a result and a project.

Most of the material on the topic is testimonial. One looksmax.org thread presents a generic 30-day plan covering a cleanser, exfoliation, moisturiser and daily sunscreen, hydration, diet, regular haircuts matched to face shape and facial-hair grooming.[1] Another user's long personal account describes being bullied in secondary school and developing an eating disorder and anxiety, then beginning filler at 16 and later adding it to the nose, cheeks, chin, lips, jaw and under-eyes, followed by rhinoplasty in May 2025.[2]

The idea of a dramatic appearance change has a long media history under the name makeover. Wikipedia describes a makeover as a radical change in appearance that may involve clothing, haircuts, cosmetics, weight loss, plastic surgery, dental veneers or contact lenses, and notes that makeovers are generally framed positively, as a way to start over.[5] In research the phrase appears occasionally; a 2024 Frontiers in Psychiatry study named a professional photoshoot intervention for adolescent psychiatric patients 'Glow up'.[3]

Wiktionary defines the noun as a dramatic positive change in someone's appearance, skills or influence, with 'glow-down' as its opposite, and lists written examples from 2017 to 2020; the verb form is thought to have come later by back-formation from the noun [9]. In the research literature on attractiveness, the modifiable features most often discussed in connection with such changes are skin condition, grooming, body composition and fitness [11].

chain: Pick changes that fit your face and routine (skin, hair, grooming, fitness, procedures)
Changes accumulate over weeks to months
angle.text: A glow up is the sum of appearance changes a person makes, from skincare and haircuts to fitness and cosmetic procedures. People document the result with comparison photos and use threads to plan the next step.

infobox: Skincare, grooming, fitness, diet, cosmetic procedures

paras: In looksmaxxing language the term runs the full range from softmaxxing (skincare, grooming, clothing, fitness, mewing-style habits) to hardmaxxing (procedures and medications). Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing describes the practice as an online self-improvement culture that emerged from message boards in the 2010s and spread widely through TikTok in the early 2020s, and lists 'ascension' among its vocabulary for a noticeable rise in looks or status [6].

Threads on looksmax.org that use the phrase include rate-me posts with a transformation attached, requests for a plan within a set time such as 14 days or 3 weeks or for 'this summer', lists of items to buy within a budget, and discussions of notable members' visible changes [1][2][4][14][15][16][17][18][19].

Wiktionary traces the noun glow-up to the pattern of words like blow-up, gives glow-down as the antonym and lists quotations from 2017 (describing a friend's improved looks and style), 2018 (a historian applying the phrase to the Byzantine empress Theodora) and 2020 (describing a garden designer's effect on estates) [9]. The page gives no first-attested date. The usage in these examples shows the word covering appearance, status and reinvention more broadly, not only looks [9].

Television has long used the format. Wikipedia lists daytime talk-show segments and series such as Queer Eye, What Not to Wear, How to Look Good Naked and Extreme Makeover among examples, and notes a recurring film trope in which a character is transformed in appearance, from Now, Voyager (1942) and My Fair Lady (1964) to Clueless (1995) and Mean Girls (2004) [5]. Virtual makeover software lets users preview cosmetics and hairstyles on photos and, in newer apps, in real time through a phone camera [5].

Extreme Makeover aired on ABC from December 11, 2002 to July 16, 2007, following participants through plastic surgery, exercise, hairdressing and wardrobe changes and ending with a reveal to family and friends [10]. Critics said the show promoted unachievable body-image goals and implied that idealised beauty could only come from cosmetic surgeons, and it was linked to a broader normalisation of cosmetic surgery [10]. Wikipedia's article on the makeover genre, by contrast, notes that makeovers are generally framed positively, as a way to start over [5].

sections.h: What changes in a glow up
paras: Skin. A common first step in forum plans and in general skin-care guidance is a basic routine. Wikipedia's skin-care article reports that dermatological consensus prioritises gentle cleansing, moisturisation and sun protection, and that chemical exfoliants are generally regarded as milder than mechanical scrubs, though over-exfoliation can irritate the skin and damage its barrier [12]. A posted 30-day plan lists exactly these elements: cleanser, exfoliation once or twice a week, moisturiser and daily sunscreen [1].

Grooming. Hair and facial hair are the most frequent items in glow-up threads. Wikipedia's attractiveness article summarises studies in which light facial hair was rated most attractive in one study, while another found Western and Oceanic women preferred clean-shaven faces but rated full beards as higher status [11].

Body and fitness. The same article cites research that body weight, waist-to-chest ratio and muscularity affect perceived attractiveness; one Australian student study found the body composition rated most attractive matched the one rated healthiest [11].

Skin glow. The attractiveness article also records that radiant, even skin may influence perceived beauty, and that redder and yellower skin tones may look healthier, while noting direct evidence linking skin colour to health is limited [11].

sections.h: Why people attach importance to it
paras: Wikipedia's attractiveness article describes the halo effect first documented by Dion, Berscheid and Walster in 1972, in which attractive people are often credited with positive traits such as intelligence and honesty, and links attractiveness to employment and social opportunities [11]. Glow-up narratives often follow that logic: members describe a change in how others respond to them after a visible transformation, and one thread asks whether people who have had a glow up feel put off when others start approaching them [8].
More broadly, personal development has become a large commercial market of books, coaching and programmes, and some scholars argue that many self-help claims lack scientific support [13].

No studies found testing 'glow up' as a looksmaxxing method. A 2024 longitudinal intervention study in Frontiers in Psychiatry examined 45 child and adolescent psychiatric patients (mean age 15.1, 30 of them female) who took part in a professional photoshoot named 'Glow up', measuring self-esteem and state emotions at five time points from one month before to three months after [3]. Significant changes in state emotions and self-esteem were found across the intervention, with boys benefiting in positive emotions and self-esteem over the longer term, and the authors suggest the 'glow up moment' during the shoot could serve as a reflection point in therapy [3]. The study examined a photoshoot rather than appearance-changing procedures, and no control group is described [3].
Separate research on social media content around eating disorder recovery analysed 150 TikTok posts under a recovery hashtag, a different topic from appearance transformation [7].

Glow-up threads on looksmax.org include requests for ratings and advice, timelines such as 14 or 30 days, and long personal accounts [1][2][15]. Titles include a thread on a member's own glow up, one about an 'accidental' glow up in someone not looksmaxxing, and a shopping list for under 1000 [14][16][17]. Some replies are sceptical; in one thread a user remarked that people claim a glow up after only improving their skin [4].

Posters also discuss how the change feels socially. One thread title asks whether people who have had a glow up feel put off when others start approaching them [8]. Wikipedia reports that critics link looksmaxxing to incel subculture and body dysmorphia concerns, and that researchers call some of its rating systems pseudoscientific, while participants frame it as self-improvement [6]. Testimonials sometimes reference bullying, insecurity and eating disorders as the background to a transformation [2].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, glow ups are shared as photo transformations and how-to lists, and debated for how real or large the change is.[1][2][4]

claims.claim: A visible glow up is achievable in 30 days through skincare, grooming, hydration and diet.
claims.believers: A posted guide lists skincare, haircuts, diet and facial hair grooming as steps for noticeable improvement in a month.[1]
claims.experts: No published studies have tested time-limited appearance plans of this kind; dermatology guidance emphasises gentle cleansing, moisturiser and sun protection as basics.[12]

claims.claim: Cosmetic procedures can transform life outcomes after a difficult adolescence.
claims.believers: One poster credits fillers and rhinoplasty with changing his life after years of bullying.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia's makeover article notes makeovers can include plastic surgery but reports no outcome research, and critics of makeover television say it implied surgery was the route to idealised beauty.[5][10]

claims.claim: Improving skin alone is enough to count as a glow up.
claims.believers: Some posters present skin-only changes as a glow up, while others are sceptical of that claim.[4]
claims.experts: No published studies define or measure a glow up; research on attractiveness lists skin condition among several modifiable features.[11]

claims.claim: Looking better changes how other people treat you.
claims.believers: Members describe changes in attention after a transformation and discuss how it feels to be approached.[8]
claims.experts: Research summarised on Wikipedia describes a halo effect in which attractive people are often credited with positive traits and linked to social and employment opportunities.[11]

claims.claim: Grooming and haircuts matched to face shape make a noticeable difference.
claims.believers: The 30-day guide advises regular haircuts suited to face shape and neat facial hair.[1]
claims.experts: Studies of facial hair preferences are mixed: light facial hair was rated most attractive in one study, while another found clean-shaven faces preferred but beards rated higher status.[11]

claims.claim: Some glow ups are smaller than they are presented as.
claims.believers: Some posters present before-and-after photos with the claim of a large change.[2][4]
claims.experts: No published studies define or measure a glow up; the question of how much of a visible change comes from skin versus other factors has not been studied.
